course.title: Darwin's Natural Selection: Reading Chapter IV of On the Origin of Species
course.description: A close study of the opening of Chapter IV of Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859), in which he defines natural selection and previews the arguments of the chapter. Learners work from Darwin's own chapter summary and first paragraph to understand how variation, heredity, and the struggle for existence combine into a principle of selection in nature, and what further consequences Darwin claims for it.

lessons.title: Darwin's Opening Question
lessons.content:
# Darwin's Opening Question

## Two questions that open Chapter IV

Chapter IV of *On the Origin of Species* begins not with a definition but with a pair of questions:

> "How will the struggle for existence, discussed too briefly in the last chapter, act in regard to variation? Can the principle of selection, which we have seen is so potent in the hands of man, apply in nature?"

Each question points backwards to a chapter Darwin has already written, and together they set up the chapter to come.

- The **struggle for existence** was the subject of Chapter III. There Darwin argued that far more individuals are born than can possibly survive, so that every organism lives under constant competition and pressure.
- The **principle of selection in the hands of man** was the subject of Chapter I, on variation under domestication. Breeders pick out the individuals with the qualities they want, breed from those, and over generations reshape pigeons, dogs, cabbages and cattle.

Darwin's move is to bring these two bodies of evidence together. Chapter III gave him a *cause of differential death*. Chapter I gave him a *model of cumulative change through selective breeding*. The question of Chapter IV is whether nature, using the first, can do what the breeder does with the second. His own answer arrives immediately and confidently: "I think we shall see that it can act most effectually."

Notice the rhetorical shape here. Darwin does not begin by asserting natural selection and then defending it. He begins by asking a question whose answer, if the premises he has already established are granted, is nearly forced. The reader is invited to draw the conclusion rather than accept it.

## The chain of premises

The rest of the opening passage is a chain, each link a thing the reader is asked to "bear in mind" or to concede as not improbable. Laid out in order:

1. **Variation is abundant.** Organisms vary in "an endless number of strange peculiarities" — greatly under domestication, and "in a lesser degree" under nature. Darwin is careful about that qualification: wild variation is real but less profuse than domestic variation. Under domestication, he says, "the whole organisation becomes in some degree plastic."
2. **Variation is inherited.** "How strong the hereditary tendency is." Without heredity, an advantageous peculiarity would die with its owner and nothing could accumulate.
3. **The relations of organisms are infinitely complex and close-fitting.** Every being stands in intricate relation to other beings and to its physical conditions. This premise does real work: in so finely meshed a world, even a slight change in a creature can matter to its fortunes.
4. **Therefore useful variations must sometimes arise.** Variations useful *to man* have undoubtedly occurred — that is a fact of the breeder's yard, not a speculation. So it cannot be thought improbable that variations useful *to the being itself*, in "the great and complex battle of life," should occur "in the course of thousands of generations."
5. **Advantage translates into survival.** Remembering that many more individuals are born than can survive, individuals with "any advantage, however slight, over others, would have the best chance of surviving and of procreating their kind." This is where Chapter III's struggle re-enters and does the selecting.
6. **Injurious variation is destroyed.** Conversely, "any variation in the least degree injurious would be rigidly destroyed."

## The definition

Only after that chain does the term appear:

> "This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection."

The definition is deliberately two-sided. Natural selection is not only the saving of the good; it is equally the rejection of the bad. And the name itself is an analogy: it is *selection*, like the breeder's, but the selecting agent is nature — that is, the conditions of life and the struggle among many more individuals than can survive.

## The third category: neutral variations

Darwin immediately marks a limit on his own principle. "Variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection, and would be left a fluctuating element, as perhaps we see in the species called polymorphic."

This is easy to skim past but important. Natural selection is not a claim that every character of every organism is useful. A variation that neither helps nor harms is invisible to selection; it simply fluctuates. Darwin offers polymorphic species — those that occur in several distinct forms — as a possible instance. The principle has a defined scope, and Darwin draws its boundary in the same paragraph in which he names it.

## Why the argument is built this way

Each premise on its own is modest, and most were already conceded by naturalists of Darwin's day. Nobody denied that domestic animals vary, that offspring resemble parents, or that most seeds and eggs perish. The force of the argument is in the assembly, not in any one plank. Darwin's phrasing keeps the burden on a sceptic: "Can it, then, be thought improbable...?" "If such do occur, can we doubt...?" To resist the conclusion, a reader must deny one of the links — and each link is hard to deny.

The chapter's summary heading tells us where this goes next: the power of natural selection compared with man's, its action on characters of trifling importance, sexual selection, the circumstances favourable and unfavourable to it, slow action, extinction, and divergence of character. But all of it rests on the chain built in this first paragraph.

lessons.content:
# Variation and the Strength of Heredity

Before Darwin can argue that nature selects, he must establish that there is something for nature to select *from*, and that whatever is selected will persist into the next generation. Chapter IV opens by asking the reader to hold three facts in mind. They are not new discoveries; they are the accumulated observations of breeders, gardeners, and naturalists, which Darwin has spent the earlier chapters assembling. Here they become the premises of an argument.

## The opening move

> "How will the struggle for existence, discussed too briefly in the last chapter, act in regard to variation? Can the principle of selection, which we have seen is so potent in the hands of man, apply in nature? I think we shall see that it can act most effectually. Let it be borne in mind in what an endless number of strange peculiarities our domestic productions, and, in a lesser degree, those under nature, vary; and how strong the hereditary tendency is."

Notice the rhetorical shape. Darwin does not begin by *proving* anything; he begins by asking his reader to *remember*. The phrase "let it be borne in mind" recurs twice in the paragraph. He is stacking already-agreed facts so that the conclusion, when it arrives, feels less like a leap than a summing-up.

## Premise 1: Domestic productions vary in an endless number of strange peculiarities

"Endless" and "strange" are doing real work. Darwin's point is not merely that pigeons differ in size, but that variation reaches into features nobody would have predicted was variable at all: the number of tail feathers in a fantail, the size of the crop in a pouter, the shape of the skull, the length of the beak, even the number of vertebrae and the proportions of the eyelids. Breeders had produced gooseberries of steadily increasing weight, cabbages differing in leaf but scarcely in flower, dogs differing in temperament as much as in bone. If variation were confined to a few obvious dimensions, selection would have only a few dimensions to work in. Because it is "endless," the raw material is effectively unrestricted.

## Premise 2: Under nature, variation is real but lesser

Darwin is careful and honest here: "and, in a lesser degree, those under nature, vary." He does not claim wild species are as variable as domestic breeds. This concession matters in two ways.

1. It is a **weakness** in the argument that he faces head-on. His opponents could say: domestic variation is a special, artificial, almost diseased condition, and nothing follows from it about wild species.
2. It is also **sufficient**. Selection does not require abundant variation; it requires *some* variation plus time. The rest of the paragraph supplies the time — "in the course of thousands of generations" — and the surplus of individuals that makes even slight differences consequential.

So the lesser degree of natural variation is compensated for, in Darwin's economy, by the vastly greater span over which nature operates.

## Premise 3: The hereditary tendency is strong

Variation alone would be useless. If a peculiarity appeared and then vanished in the offspring, no amount of preservation could accumulate it. Darwin therefore couples variation with heredity in a single clause: "how strong the hereditary tendency is." Notice he says *tendency*, not law. He had no mechanism — no genes, no Mendel — only the breeders' massive practical experience that like tends to beget like, and that novelties, once they appear, can be fixed by breeding from them. Selection is an accumulating process, and heredity is what allows the accumulation to hold.

## Premise 4: The whole organisation becomes plastic

> "Under domestication, it may be truly said that the whole organisation becomes in some degree plastic."

This is the most sweeping of the four claims, and the qualifiers deserve attention: *in some degree*, and *under domestication*. Darwin is not saying an organism can be moulded into anything at will. He is saying that no part of the organisation is off-limits to variation — not internal organs, not instincts, not the timing of development. Nothing is locked. Against a view in which each species has a fixed essential form with only superficial features free to wobble, this claim removes the boundary between trivial and fundamental characters.

## Where the premises lead

With these in hand, Darwin poses his question as one about probability rather than proof:

> "Can it, then, be thought improbable, seeing that variations useful to man have undoubtedly occurred, that other variations useful in some way to each being in the great and complex battle of life, should sometimes occur in the course of thousands of generations?"

The inference runs: variations useful *to man* demonstrably occur; usefulness to man is an arbitrary, narrow criterion; so variations useful *to the organism itself* should occur too, given enough generations. Add the fact that many more individuals are born than can survive, and any advantage "however slight" gives its bearer the best chance of surviving and reproducing, while "any variation in the least degree injurious would be rigidly destroyed." That two-sided process — preservation of the favourable, rejection of the injurious — is what Darwin names Natural Selection.

## The neutral remainder

One consequence is easy to overlook. Darwin immediately adds: "Variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection, and would be left a fluctuating element, as perhaps we see in the species called polymorphic." Selection is not a universal solvent. It grips only what makes a difference to survival and reproduction; everything else drifts unfixed. Darwin's theory thus predicts pockets of unexplained, unstable variability, and he points to polymorphic species as a possible case. It is a small but telling instance of a theory being strengthened by specifying what it does *not* explain.

## Summary of the logical skeleton

| Premise | Role in the argument |
|---|---|
| Endless strange peculiarities under domestication | Supplies unlimited raw material |
| Lesser but real variation under nature | Extends the raw material to wild species |
| Strong hereditary tendency | Allows selected differences to accumulate |
| Whole organisation plastic in some degree | Removes any part from being exempt from change |
| Many more born than can survive | Makes slight advantages decisive |

Remove any one of these and the argument stalls. Together, they make natural selection look less like a bold hypothesis and more like an inevitability.

# Complex and Close-Fitting Relations

## The sentence at the hinge of the argument

Early in Chapter IV of *On the Origin of Species*, Darwin asks whether the principle of selection, so powerful in the hands of breeders, can also operate in nature. Before he answers, he asks the reader to hold three things in mind. The third is this:

> "Let it be borne in mind how infinitely complex and close-fitting are the mutual relations of all organic beings to each other and to their physical conditions of life."

This is not decorative language. It is a load-bearing premise. Everything Darwin says afterwards about natural selection depends on it, and it is worth slowing down to see exactly what work it does.

## Unpacking the phrase

Two adjectives do the work, and they pull in different directions.

**Complex.** The relations are many, and they run in many directions. A being is related to *other organic beings* — its prey, its predators, its parasites, its competitors, the plants it shelters under, the insects that pollinate it — and also to its *physical conditions of life* — temperature, moisture, soil, light, season. No organism sits in a simple two-term relationship with its world. It sits at the intersection of an enormous number of them.

**Close-fitting.** The relations are not loose. They are snug, like a joint in cabinetry. A small alteration in one part is felt in another. Because the fit is tight, a slight change in a beak, a root hair, a coat colour, a hatching date, is *the kind of thing that can matter*. In a loose-jointed world, small differences would rattle around without consequence.

Put the two together and you get Darwin's point: there are an enormous number of ways for an organism to be related to its surroundings, and each of those relations is tight enough that a small variation could improve or worsen it.

## Why this makes useful variation plausible

Darwin's argument here is an argument from plausibility, and it is built as an analogy with an added premise.

The analogy: variations useful *to man* have undoubtedly occurred. Breeders did not manufacture the woolly fleece or the fantail pigeon; they found small differences already present and accumulated them. Under domestication, Darwin notes, "the whole organisation becomes in some degree plastic" — variation appears in an endless number of strange peculiarities, and the hereditary tendency is strong.

The question: if useful-to-man variations occur, why should useful-to-the-organism variations not occur too?

The added premise — and this is where complexity and close fit come in — answers an objection. One might reply: *man has a specific goal in mind, and he keeps only what serves it; nature has no goal, so "useful" has no meaning outside the breeder's yard.* Darwin's premise blocks this. Because a being stands in infinitely complex and close-fitting relations, there are countless respects in which a variation could be useful — better at escaping, at digesting, at withstanding drought, at attracting a pollinator, at surviving a cold week in March. Usefulness in nature is not narrow; it is *broader* than the breeder's usefulness, because the relations are more numerous than any breeder's list of desiderata.

Hence the rhetorical question:

> "Can it, then, be thought improbable... that other variations useful in some way to each being in the great and complex battle of life, should sometimes occur in the course of thousands of generations?"

Note the modesty of the claim. Darwin does not say useful variations are common, or that they appear on demand. He says they should *sometimes* occur, over *thousands of generations*. He is asking only that we grant an occasional occurrence over a very long stretch of time. The complexity premise makes that concession look cheap: with so many close-fitting relations, it would be strange if no variation ever happened to improve one of them.

## What follows once the concession is granted

With useful variations conceded, Darwin brings in the result of the previous chapter — many more individuals are born than can possibly survive. Given that surplus, an individual with any advantage, "however slight," has the best chance of surviving and of leaving offspring. Conversely, "any variation in the least degree injurious would be rigidly destroyed."

This two-sided process — **the preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations** — is what Darwin names *natural selection*.

The argument therefore runs in a chain:

1. Organisms vary, and variation is inherited.
2. Relations to other beings and to physical conditions are infinitely complex and close-fitting.
3. Therefore some variations will, from time to time, be useful in the battle of life.
4. Far more individuals are born than can survive.
5. Therefore the useful variants are preserved and the injurious destroyed: natural selection.

Remove step 2 and step 3 has no support; the analogy with the breeder collapses into the objection that nature has no purposes.

## The third category: neither useful nor injurious

Darwin adds a careful qualification that is easy to skip. Natural selection acts on favourable and on injurious variations. But variations that are **neither useful nor injurious** are *not* acted on by it at all. They are "left a fluctuating element," and Darwin suggests we may see this in the species called **polymorphic** — species that show several persistent forms without any one of them being weeded out.

This matters for two reasons. First, it shows Darwin does not claim that every character of every organism has been shaped for advantage. Second, it makes his theory falsifiable in principle: selection has a specific domain, and indifferent variation lies outside it.

## An illustration

Consider a flowering plant. Its relations include: the depth of soil moisture it can reach; the beetles that eat its leaves; the fungus on its roots; the bees that carry its pollen; the date of the last frost; the neighbouring plants shading it; the birds that disperse its seeds.

Now imagine a small heritable variation — a slightly longer corolla tube. In a world of loose relations, this would be an irrelevant detail. In a close-fitting world it is not: it may exclude a short-tongued nectar thief while still admitting the long-tongued bee that actually transfers pollen. That is a use nobody designed and no breeder sought. And because the plant stands in *many* such relations, there are many such chances — which is precisely why, over thousands of generations, useful variations should sometimes turn up.

## Reading note

Darwin's prose here is a sequence of rhetorical questions: "Can it, then, be thought improbable...?" "If such do occur, can we doubt...?" He is not proving a theorem. He is shifting the burden: given plastic organisms, strong heredity, close-fitting relations, and overproduction of offspring, the sceptic must explain why useful variation would *never* occur and why, if it did, it would *not* be preserved.

# Preservation and Rejection

## The sentence that names the theory

In Chapter IV of *On the Origin of Species*, after several pages of preparation, Darwin finally writes the definition:

> "This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection."

Notice what kind of sentence this is. It is not a discovery announcement ("I have found a force in nature"). It is a **naming**: Darwin points back at a process he has just argued must happen, and gives it a label. The word "call" matters. Everything that licenses the theory has already been said in the preceding sentences; the name is a convenience for talking about it afterwards.

Notice too that the definition has **two halves**, not one. Natural selection is *preservation* of the favourable **and** *rejection* of the injurious. Popular summaries often keep only the first half — "the fittest survive" — but Darwin's process is two-sided, and the destructive half is the one he states with the most confidence.

## The argument, step by step

Darwin's paragraph is a chain of conditionals. Laid out as premises:

1. **Organisms vary.** Under domestication, "the whole organisation becomes in some degree plastic"; in nature, variation is smaller but real. Darwin appeals to "an endless number of strange peculiarities" in domestic productions and, "in a lesser degree," in wild ones.
2. **Variation is inherited.** "How strong the hereditary tendency is." Without heredity, an advantage would die with its possessor.
3. **Relations between organisms are "infinitely complex and close-fitting."** Because each being is tightly meshed with other beings and with its physical conditions, there are countless ways in which a small change could matter — countless narrow margins on which a slight difference could tell.
4. **Some variations will therefore be useful to their possessors.** This step is an analogy plus a probability claim: variations useful *to man* have undoubtedly occurred (that is what breeders exploit), so over "thousands of generations" it is not improbable that variations useful *to the organism itself* should sometimes occur.
5. **Many more individuals are born than can possibly survive.** This is the conclusion of the previous chapter, the struggle for existence, imported here as the engine.
6. **Therefore** individuals with "any advantage, however slight, over others, would have the best chance of surviving and of procreating their kind."
7. **Conversely**, "any variation in the least degree injurious would be rigidly destroyed."

Steps 6 and 7 together are what step 8 names: natural selection.

## Why superabundance of births is the hinge

Strip out premise 5 and the argument collapses. If every individual born survived and bred, a slight advantage would confer nothing: the advantaged and the disadvantaged would both leave offspring, and no sorting would occur. Advantage only converts into differential survival when there is a **shortage of places** — when some must die.

Darwin flags this dependence with a parenthesis that is easy to read past: "can we doubt (**remembering that many more individuals are born than can possibly survive**) that individuals having any advantage..." The bracket carries the whole weight. Overproduction turns life into a competition with fixed seats, and any tiny edge becomes a better ticket.

This also explains the strength of the phrase **"however slight."** In a world of scarce places, an advantage does not need to be large or obvious to be selected. It only needs to shift the odds. Compounded across generations, an edge too small for a naturalist to notice in one individual can still be decisive for a lineage.

## Asymmetry of confidence

Read Darwin's verbs closely. For the preservation half he asks a rhetorical question — "can we doubt...?" — and awards the advantaged individual only "the **best chance** of surviving." It is a claim about probabilities, not guarantees. A superior individual can still be crushed by a falling branch.

For the rejection half his language hardens: "we may **feel sure** that any variation in the least degree injurious would be **rigidly destroyed**." "Rigidly" and "destroyed" are unsparing words. Darwin is more certain of elimination than of promotion, and that asymmetry is deliberate: killing off the unfit is a blunt, reliable operation, while the spread of a favourable variant depends on chance, numbers, and time.

## The third category: neither useful nor injurious

Darwin immediately adds a limitation that is part of the definition's precision:

> "Variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection, and would be left a fluctuating element, as perhaps we see in the species called polymorphic."

So variations fall into three classes, not two:

| Class | Fate under natural selection |
|---|---|
| Favourable | Preserved |
| Injurious | Rejected ("rigidly destroyed") |
| Neither | **Untouched** — left fluctuating |

This is a statement about the theory's **scope**. Natural selection is not a universal explainer of every trait; it has no grip on differences that make no difference to survival. Darwin cites *polymorphic* species — species in which two or more distinct forms persist side by side — as the visible symptom of such indifference. Where selection is silent, variability is free to wander.

That concession is a strength, not a weakness. A principle that claimed to shape every character would be untestable; by specifying what it does *not* do, Darwin makes it an explanation with edges.

## Selection selects nothing

One last point of vocabulary. The chapter opens by asking whether "the principle of selection, which we have seen is so potent in the hands of man, apply in nature." The analogy with the breeder is Darwin's rhetorical bridge — but the definition itself contains no chooser. Preservation and rejection are outcomes of differential survival among crowded, varying, heritable organisms. Nothing inspects the variations and approves them; the ones that hinder their bearers are simply removed by the ordinary mortality that scarcity guarantees.

## Checking your grasp

Ask yourself of any purported example of natural selection:

- Is the trait **variable**, and is the variation **inherited**?
- Are more individuals born than can survive, so that places are scarce?
- Does the trait make even a slight difference to the chance of surviving and *procreating* — not merely of surviving?

If the answer to the last question is no, Darwin's own text tells you to expect the trait to fluctuate freely rather than be shaped.

lessons.title: Neutral Variation and Polymorphic Species
lessons.content:
# Neutral Variation and Polymorphic Species

## The sentence that is easy to skip

At the end of the paragraph in which Darwin first names his theory, he writes:

> "This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection. Variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection, and would be left a fluctuating element, as perhaps we see in the species called polymorphic."

Readers usually stop at the first sentence — the famous definition. The second sentence is a qualification, and it does something important: it draws a boundary around the theory. Darwin is telling us, in the very moment of naming his mechanism, what his mechanism does **not** do.

## Three fates, not two

Darwin's definition sorts variations into categories by their consequences for the individual's chance of surviving and reproducing:

1. **Useful variations** — "individuals having any advantage, however slight, over others, would have the best chance of surviving and of procreating their kind." These are *preserved*.
2. **Injurious variations** — "any variation in the least degree injurious would be rigidly destroyed." These are *rejected*.
3. **Variations neither useful nor injurious** — these are simply *not affected*. Selection has no purchase on them, because nothing about them changes an organism's odds in the struggle for existence.

Notice that natural selection, as Darwin defines it, is a *two-sided* filter: it is both the preservation of the good and the rejection of the bad. Both sides depend on the variation making some difference to survival or reproduction. Where a variation makes no such difference, neither side of the filter engages.

## "A fluctuating element"

What happens to a variation that selection ignores? Darwin says it is "left a fluctuating element." The phrase is worth unpacking.

*Left* — that is, abandoned by the mechanism; selection does not drive it in either direction. It is not preserved and it is not destroyed.

*Fluctuating* — it wobbles. Such a character has no tendency to be steadily improved, steadily eliminated, or steadily held constant. It may be common in one generation and rarer in the next, for reasons unconnected with its usefulness. The result within a species is variability that persists rather than variability that gets resolved into one winning form.

So Darwin predicts a *pattern* here, not just an absence. If some characters are invisible to selection, we should expect to find species that carry several forms of a character at once, with no evident advantage to any of them.

## Polymorphic species

"Polymorphic" means many-formed. Darwin uses the word for those species which naturalists of his day found frustrating: species in which individuals differ conspicuously from one another in some character — colouring, shell banding, the shape of a leaf or a plume — without those differences sorting the species into recognisable, geographically distinct varieties, and without any of the forms appearing better fitted than the others.

Darwin's suggestion is that these species may be exactly what his theory predicts: cases where the varying character happens to be neither useful nor injurious, so nothing has ever pruned the variation away.

Two things about how he says it:

- **He is tentative.** "As perhaps we see" — he offers polymorphic species as a possible illustration, not as proof. He is not claiming to have demonstrated that any particular character is neutral; showing that a trait has *no* effect on survival is far harder than showing that it has one.
- **He offers a candidate explanation, not a new mechanism.** Neutrality is not a second force acting alongside selection. It is the description of what a variation looks like when the one force he has described does not apply to it.

## Why the qualification matters

A common caricature of Darwinism holds that every feature of every organism must be an adaptation, present because it earned its keep. That caricature is not available to a careful reader of Chapter IV, because Darwin explicitly denies it on the same page where he introduces natural selection. Some features may simply be *there*.

The qualification also protects the theory from a bad kind of unfalsifiability. If every character had to be useful, then a naturalist confronted with a puzzling trait would be obliged to invent a use for it. Darwin's third category means the honest answer "this may make no difference at all" is a legitimate option, and it makes the theory sharper rather than weaker: natural selection claims to explain the *fit* between organism and conditions of life, not every last detail of form.

One caution when applying the idea. Neutrality is not a permanent property of a trait. Whether a variation is useful, injurious, or indifferent depends on "the infinitely complex and close-fitting" relations between the organism, other organisms, and its physical conditions. Change the conditions and a character that was a fluctuating element may become the difference between surviving and not. Neutrality is a relation to circumstances, not a fixed label.

## A worked example of the reasoning

Suppose a snail species shows shells with three, four, or five dark bands, in stable proportions, across a wide range of habitats.

- If banding affected how easily predators spotted the snail, we would expect selection to preserve the better-concealed pattern and rigidly destroy the worse — the variation should be reduced over generations.
- If instead the banding is invisible to predators and irrelevant to everything else in the snail's life, no such pruning occurs. The proportions drift about; all three forms persist. The species looks polymorphic.

The persistence of the several forms is therefore *evidence bearing on* neutrality — but only weak evidence, since a character can also be maintained in several forms for reasons Darwin discusses elsewhere. This is why he wrote "perhaps."

lessons.title: Nature's Selection Compared with Man's
lessons.content:
# Nature's Selection Compared with Man's

## The chapter's own signpost

Darwin opens Chapter IV of *On the Origin of Species* with a dense list of topics — a kind of table of contents for the chapter:

> "Natural Selection: its power compared with man's selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes. Sexual Selection. On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species..."

The first three items in that list are all comparisons. Darwin is not announcing a brand-new force; he is announcing that a process already familiar to his readers — the selection practised by pigeon-fanciers, sheep-breeders and gardeners — has a wild counterpart, and that the wild counterpart is the *stronger* of the two. This lesson unpacks that comparison.

## The argument by analogy

Chapter I of the *Origin* was about variation under domestication; Chapter III was about the struggle for existence. Chapter IV joins them:

> "How will the struggle for existence... act in regard to variation? Can the principle of selection, which we have seen is so potent in the hands of man, apply in nature? I think we shall see that it can act most effectually."

The argument runs through four premises, each of which Darwin asks the reader to "bear in mind":

1. **Organisms vary** — in "an endless number of strange peculiarities" under domestication, and, importantly, "in a lesser degree" in nature too. Under domestication "the whole organisation becomes in some degree plastic."
2. **Variation is inherited** — "how strong the hereditary tendency is."
3. **Life is a web of tight relationships** — "how infinitely complex and close-fitting are the mutual relations of all organic beings to each other and to their physical conditions of life." Because the fit is so close, even a small change can matter.
4. **More are born than can live** — "many more individuals are born than can possibly survive."

From these he draws the conclusion. If variations useful *to man* have undoubtedly occurred, is it improbable that variations useful *to the organism itself* should occur over thousands of generations? And if they do occur, can we doubt that "individuals having any advantage, however slight, over others, would have the best chance of surviving and of procreating their kind"? Meanwhile "any variation in the least degree injurious would be rigidly destroyed."

Notice what the analogy actually does. Artificial selection is not the *cause* of natural selection, nor is it evidence that natural selection occurs. It is a *proof of concept*: it shows that picking and breeding from slight differences, repeated over generations, can reshape a lineage dramatically. Darwin's job is then to argue that nature does the picking.

## The definition

> "This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection."

Two halves, and both matter. Natural selection is not only the preservation of the good; it is equally the destruction of the harmful. And the criterion of "favourable" is not beauty, complexity, or human usefulness — it is advantage to the individual in "the great and complex battle of life."

The word "selection" is a metaphor borrowed from the breeder, and Darwin knew it invited misreading (in later editions he added Spencer's phrase "survival of the fittest" as a synonym). There is no selector in nature. What there is, is differential survival and reproduction among varying, heritable individuals.

## Where the two processes differ

**Whose good?** The breeder selects for his own benefit or fancy — more wool, sweeter fruit, a fantail's plumage. Nature selects only for the good of the organism possessing the variation. A pouter pigeon is a triumph for the fancier and a liability in the wild.

**Trifling characters.** This is Darwin's boldest claim in the chapter heading, and it turns the comparison in nature's favour. A breeder can only select for differences he can *see* and *cares about*. Nature scrutinises everything. An advantage "however slight" — a marginally thicker down, a seed hair a little better at catching wind, a tint of colour that hides a caterpillar for one extra second — is enough, because in a struggle where most individuals die, a tiny difference in the chance of dying is compounded over enormous numbers and enormous stretches of time. Characters that look trifling to *us* may be decisive in the "close-fitting" relations of item 3 above.

**Reach.** Man works chiefly on outward, visible, saleable structures. Nature works on the whole machinery of life, including internal organs, physiology and instinct — anything that touches survival or reproduction.

**Age and sex.** Breeders typically select at one convenient stage (an adult animal at market weight, a ripened fruit) and often on one sex. Nature acts "at all ages and on both sexes": an egg, a larva, a seedling and a senescent adult are all exposed to the struggle, and a variation that helps only at the larval stage is preserved just as readily as one that helps in adulthood. This is why natural selection can mould life-histories — caterpillars as well as butterflies — while artificial selection tends to sculpt the stage the breeder looks at.

**Time.** The breeder works within a human lifetime; nature works over geological ages. Slow action is one of Darwin's later headings in the same chapter.

## What natural selection does *not* touch

Darwin is careful to bound his mechanism:

> "Variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection, and would be left a fluctuating element, as perhaps we see in the species called polymorphic."

This is an important qualification, and modern readers should notice how much it anticipates. A variation with no effect on survival is invisible to selection; it simply fluctuates. Darwin's suggested example is *polymorphic* species — those that occur in several forms at once, with no form apparently favoured. Today we would speak of neutral variation and genetic drift; Darwin had no theory of why neutral variants persist, only the honesty to say that selection does not explain them.

## Summary

Darwin's comparison is not "nature is like a breeder." It is: nature does what a breeder does, but more thoroughly, on more characters, at every age, in both sexes, for the organism's own good, and for immeasurably longer. The breeder is the small, visible, human-scale demonstration of a principle whose full form is invisible because it is too slow and too fine-grained to watch.

lessons.content:
# Sexual Selection and Intercrossing

## Reading the chapter's own table of contents

Darwin opens Chapter IV with a compressed list of everything the chapter will cover. It reads almost like a syllabus:

> Natural Selection: its power compared with man's selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes. **Sexual Selection. On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species.** Circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection, namely, **intercrossing**, isolation, number of individuals. Slow action. Extinction... Divergence of Character...

Two things in that list concern us here, and it is worth noticing that they sit side by side. First, **sexual selection**. Second, **the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species** — which then reappears a few clauses later as the first item under "circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection."

Why should a book about the origin of species devote so much of one chapter to who mates with whom? Because, for Darwin, breeding relations are not a side topic. They are the machinery through which selection does anything at all.

## Selection is settled in offspring, not in deaths

Here is Darwin's core statement of the principle, and it repays close reading:

> If such do occur, can we doubt (remembering that many more individuals are born than can possibly survive) that individuals having any advantage, however slight, over others, would have the best chance of **surviving and of procreating their kind**? On the other hand, we may feel sure that any variation in the least degree injurious would be rigidly destroyed. This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection.

Note the pairing: *surviving and of procreating their kind*. Survival alone changes nothing heritable. An animal that outlives every rival but leaves no descendants has contributed exactly as much to the future of its species as one that died young. A variation only counts as "preserved" if it is passed on. So the whole theory rests on a reproductive bookkeeping, and any fact about how a species breeds — whether the sexes compete, whether individuals cross with each other or self-fertilise — is a fact about how, and how fast, selection can work.

Darwin also marks out what selection does *not* touch:

> Variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection, and would be left a fluctuating element, as perhaps we see in the species called polymorphic.

A neutral character is invisible to selection. It is neither preserved nor rejected, so it drifts about unsettled, differing from individual to individual — Darwin's suggested explanation for **polymorphic** species, those that vary wildly in some feature without any of the variants seeming to matter.

## Sexual selection: a second kind of struggle

Darwin's chapter heading notes that natural selection acts "at all ages and on both sexes," and then immediately names **Sexual Selection** as a separate heading. It is separate because the struggle involved is of a different kind.

Ordinary natural selection turns on the struggle for existence: the loser dies, or fails to find food, or is eaten. Sexual selection turns on a struggle between individuals of one sex — generally the males — for possession of the other sex. The penalty for losing is not death. The loser simply leaves few or no offspring.

That is a milder penalty in one sense and just as decisive in another, since it is offspring that keep the score. And it explains a class of characters that pure survival cannot: the stag's antlers, the cock's spurs, the peacock's train, the song of male birds. Some of these are weapons for direct combat with rivals; others are charms, of no use in a fight, which work only because they attract females. Several are positively inconvenient for staying alive — a bright plumage is easier for a hawk to spot. They persist because the advantage in breeding outweighs the disadvantage in surviving. This is also why sexual selection typically produces differences *between* the sexes within one species, rather than modifying the whole species alike.

## The generality of intercrosses

The second topic is factual before it is theoretical: does each individual of a species habitually breed with another individual, or can it breed with itself?

For animals with separate sexes the answer is trivially yes — a cross is unavoidable. The interesting cases are hermaphrodites, especially plants with both stamens and pistils in one flower, which look as though they could dispense with a partner entirely. Darwin's contention, argued at length in the chapter, is that even here an occasional cross with a distinct individual is very nearly a universal law of nature: the elaborate arrangements of flowers, the behaviour of insects that visit them, and the general vigour of crossed offspring all point the same way.

Why labour the point? Because it means that no individual is reproductively an island. Every new favourable variation, when it arises, will be mixed with the constitutions of unmodified neighbours.

## Why intercrossing is listed twice — as favourable *and* unfavourable

This is the subtlety worth carrying away from the lesson. Intercrossing appears in the chapter heading under *both* halves of "circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection." It cuts both ways.

- **Favourable.** Crossing keeps the individuals of a species true to one common character and gives crossed offspring vigour. It also spreads a new advantageous variation through a population instead of confining it to a single family line, so that selection has a supply of modified individuals to work on.
- **Unfavourable.** Free crossing with the ordinary, unmodified form continually blends a new variation back towards the average. A single well-endowed individual in a large freely-crossing population is in danger of having its peculiarity diluted away in a few generations.

This is exactly why the chapter heading places intercrossing next to **isolation** and **number of individuals**. Isolation restricts crossing, and so protects a nascent variety from being swamped; a large number of individuals supplies more variations to select from. The three conditions have to be weighed against one another. Breeding relations, in short, are not background detail — they set the terms on which every other part of the argument operates.

## Summary

- Natural selection is *the preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations*; neutral variations are untouched and left fluctuating, as in polymorphic species.
- The test is surviving **and** procreating: variations are preserved only through offspring, which makes breeding relations central.
- Sexual selection is a distinct mode, depending on a struggle between individuals of one sex for mates; the penalty for failure is few or no offspring rather than death, and it can favour characters that are useless or even harmful for survival.
- Crossing between distinct individuals of the same species is very general, even among hermaphrodites — and it both spreads new variations and threatens to blend them away, which is why Darwin treats it as at once favourable and unfavourable to selection.

lessons.title: Conditions, Slowness, and Extinction
lessons.content:
# Conditions, Slowness, and Extinction

Darwin's summary of Chapter IV promises to discuss "Circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection, namely, intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals. Slow action. Extinction caused by Natural Selection." Having argued that selection *can* act in nature, he now asks a more practical question: **when does it act well, when badly, how fast, and at whose expense?**

His answer is unsentimental. Natural selection is not a force that operates everywhere at full strength. It is throttled or assisted by demography and geography; it works at a pace no human observer could ever watch; and every success it produces is paid for by the destruction of something else.

---

## 1. Intercrossing: the levelling force

Darwin had just spent several pages arguing that crossing between individuals is far more general in nature than naturalists supposed — even among hermaphrodites, an occasional cross seems to be the rule. That conclusion matters here, because free intercrossing has a definite effect on selection.

Suppose a favourable variation appears in one individual of a large, freely-breeding, wandering population. Its offspring will not breed among themselves in a private corner; they will mate with the unmodified majority. Each generation the peculiarity is blended back towards the average. Darwin's verdict is that **intercrossing keeps the individuals of a species uniform in character**. Uniformity is exactly what a modifying process does not want.

But the effect is double-edged, and Darwin says so:

- **Against modification:** blending swamps incipient varieties and prevents a local population from drifting away from the rest of the species.
- **For improvement:** the same blending *spreads* an advantage. Once a useful variation is common enough to resist swamping, crossing diffuses it through the whole population rather than confining it to one family line.

So intercrossing is unfavourable to *divergence* into new forms while being favourable to the *uniform improvement* of an existing one. Anything that checks free crossing — a barrier, a habit of staying put, self-fertilisation — makes the formation of a distinct new variety easier.

---

## 2. Isolation: important, but not simply good

Isolation is the most obvious check on intercrossing, and Darwin treats it as "an important element" in the process. Its advantages:

1. It prevents crossing with the unmodified stock outside.
2. In a confined area the physical and organic conditions tend to be **uniform**, so selection pushes all the individuals in the same direction rather than in a dozen conflicting ones.
3. It excludes immigration. Better-adapted invaders cannot arrive and seize the places in the economy of nature, so those places are left open for the old inhabitants to be slowly modified into.

Its great disadvantage is arithmetic: **a small isolated area contains few individuals.** And that, for Darwin, brings us to the third condition.

---

## 3. Number of individuals

Natural selection cannot select what has not appeared. Variations are not produced to order; they turn up, rarely, and by chance with respect to what is needed. Therefore the chance that a *useful* variation appears within any given stretch of time depends on how many individuals there are to vary. Darwin calls a large number of individuals a highly important element of success.

This is why the advantage of isolation is bought at a price. An island may keep its inhabitants pure and undisturbed, but with only a few thousand individuals it may wait a very long time before the right variation shows up at all. Isolation gives selection a clean workshop with very little raw material.

---

## 4. Small isolated areas versus large open areas

Darwin's conclusion balances the two. Small isolated areas — islands, lakes, mountain-tops — do produce **peculiar, endemic forms**, because crossing is checked and conditions are uniform. But large continental areas are, in the long run, the more powerful nursery of new species that *endure and spread*, because they offer:

- great numbers of individuals, hence many variations;
- many already-existing species, hence severe and varied competition;
- conditions that change over vast tracts, and areas that are repeatedly broken up and rejoined by geological change.

A form that has been forged in that severe competition, when it does escape its home, tends to beat the products of small isolated regions. Hence, Darwin says, continental productions are dominant and widely-spread, while island productions, though peculiar, are vulnerable.

---

## 5. Slow action

Darwin insists on slowness, and he insists on it for a specific reason, not merely out of caution. Natural selection can only act **when there are places in the polity of nature that could be better filled** by modifying some existing inhabitant. Whether such places exist depends on slow changes: slow changes of climate, the occasional arrival of immigrants, and the gradual modification of the other inhabitants. So selection "will generally act very slowly, often only at long intervals of time, and generally on only a very few of the inhabitants of the same region at the same time."

Two consequences follow.

- **We should not expect to see it.** A human life, or the whole span of recorded history, is far too short. We perceive nothing of these slow changes in progress until the hand of time has marked the long lapse of ages.
- **The argument depends on geology.** Darwin's case rests on the Lyellian view of an immensely old earth changing by small accumulated steps. A reader who rejects the vastness of geological time will reject natural selection with it.

---

## 6. Extinction, the shadow of selection

Natural selection acts solely by preserving profitable variations. Every preserved variant occupies a place; every place it occupies is a place denied to something else. Darwin therefore treats extinction not as an unfortunate side-effect but as the necessary partner of improvement: **as new forms are produced, others must become rarer and finally disappear.**

The crucial refinement is *which* forms disappear. The struggle is severest between organisms that are most alike, because they have the most nearly identical needs — the same food, the same shelter, the same enemies. Therefore:

- an improved variety tends first to exterminate **its own parent form**;
- next, the other varieties of the same species;
- next, the other species of the same genus, its closest relatives.

Rarity is the warning sign: a form becomes rare before it becomes extinct, and we notice the rarity without much surprise, though it is the beginning of an execution.

### A worked illustration

Imagine a wide continent with a large population of a browsing mammal. Numbers are great, so variations in leg length appear often; the region is broken by rivers, so some populations are partly isolated and can diverge without being swamped by crossing; competition is severe, so any slight advantage matters. Over an immense period a longer-legged form spreads. It does not merely add itself to the fauna — it competes hardest with the medium-legged parent stock it most resembles, and that stock grows rare and vanishes. The result is a gap: a distinct new species, with no surviving intermediates, the intermediates having been destroyed by the very process that produced their successor.

That single picture contains all of the lesson's elements — numbers supplying variation, partial isolation permitting divergence, immense time permitting accumulation, and extinction of the nearest relatives writing the result into the record.

lessons.title: Divergence of Character and the Grouping of Organic Beings
lessons.content:
# Divergence of Character and the Grouping of Organic Beings

Chapter IV opens with the definition of natural selection itself: "This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection." Variations that are neither useful nor injurious escape its action and remain "a fluctuating element." But by the end of the chapter Darwin is after something larger. Natural selection explains adaptation; it does not, by itself, obviously explain why life comes packaged in *groups within groups* — species inside genera, genera inside families, families inside orders. To get there Darwin adds a second principle, announced in his own chapter summary as "Divergence of Character, related to the diversity of inhabitants of any small area, and to naturalisation. Action of Natural Selection, through Divergence of Character and Extinction, on the descendants from a common parent. Explains the Grouping of all organic beings."

This lesson follows that final chain of argument, link by link.

---

## 1. The problem: why should varieties diverge at all?

Breeders supply the first clue. Two fanciers start with the same rock-pigeon; one prefers a slightly shorter beak, the other a slightly longer one. Neither wants a middling bird. Over generations the two lines walk away from each other and from the parent stock, and the intermediate birds simply stop being bred. Darwin's question is what plays the part of the fancier's *preference* in nature — what makes descendants of one parent species drift apart instead of merely getting better at the same single job.

His answer is that **the more diversified the descendants of any one species become in structure, constitution, and habits, the better able they will be to seize on many and widely different places in the polity of nature, and so the more of them can live.** Divergence is not a taste; it is a route to greater numbers. A carnivorous quadruped already at the limit of what a district will support can only multiply further if some of its descendants take prey the others neglect, hunt at other hours, or enter new ground. Every step away from a sibling's way of life is a step out of direct competition with the closest, fiercest competitor a being has.

Notice the shape of this reasoning. Competition is keenest between the most similar forms, because they want the same things. Therefore the extremes of any variable species suffer least from it, and natural selection tends to preserve the extremes at the expense of the mean.

---

## 2. First support: the diversity of inhabitants of any small area

If diversity itself lets more life be supported, then a small patch of ground should hold beings that are not merely numerous but *taxonomically scattered*. Darwin looked. On a plot of turf three feet by four he counted twenty species of plant, and these belonged to eighteen genera and eight orders — a level of dissimilarity out of all proportion to the plot's size. Sown with several distinct genera of grasses, a piece of ground yields a greater weight of herbage than the same ground sown with a single species. The greatest amount of life can be supported by the greatest diversification of structure.

Darwin borrows a phrase from the physiologist Milne Edwards to name the analogy: **the physiological division of labour**. A stomach that only digests vegetable matter, or only flesh, draws more nutriment from that matter than a stomach of mixed capacities; likewise, in the economy of a district, specialists collectively extract more than generalists all doing the same job badly. It is worth being clear that this is offered as an *analogy* that makes the principle intelligible, alongside the counts of species and the sowing trials, which are the evidence proper.

---

## 3. Second support: naturalisation

Here the argument is subtler and easy to get backwards. When plants and animals from abroad establish themselves in a new land, one might expect the successful invaders to be close relatives of the natives — forms already proven to suit the country. What Darwin finds is the opposite tendency: the naturalised productions of any land belong, in a large proportion, to **genera that contain no native species at all** — a much higher proportion of new *genera* than one would predict from the proportion of new *species* they represent.

Why? Because a foreign form very like the natives must fight them for the very place they already occupy, whereas a form widely unlike anything present can slip into a place in the polity of nature that no resident is filling. The naturalisation record is thus a large, unplanned experiment confirming what the turf plot suggested: dissimilar forms coexist most easily, and dissimilarity is what wins entry.

---

## 4. Divergence plus extinction, acting on descendants of a common parent

Darwin now runs the two principles together in his one diagram. Imagine a species, A, of a large genus in a wide-ranging land. Its varieties are shown fanning out; at each interval of many generations, the varieties that have diverged most are the ones preserved and continued, while the intermediate varieties — fewer in number, squeezed between two better-fitted extremes — leave no continuation. After thousands of generations A has produced several well-marked varieties, then species; after more, whole clusters of species; and the earliest branches, if not extinguished, sit far below and far apart from the modern twigs.

Two consequences follow, and both are essential.

**(a) Extinction is not an accidental extra; it is the other half of the mechanism.** As improved descendants of A multiply and spread, the forms they most resemble and most closely compete with are exterminated first — their own parent form, their own intermediate varieties, and the less improved species of the same genus. Natural selection and extinction are, as Darwin puts it, hand in hand.

**(b) The gaps in nature are made, not given.** Because it is precisely the intermediate links that get destroyed, the surviving forms stand apart in distinct clusters, with blanks where connecting forms once lived. If every intermediate had been preserved, we should see an unbroken gradation and no clean species boundaries at all.

Meanwhile some species, like the diagram's F, may persist for immense periods unchanged, in a protected or unusual station, having never been forced to diverge — which is why isolated, relatively unaltered forms still exist beside teeming modern groups.

---

## 5. What this explains: the grouping of all organic beings

Now the payoff. Run divergence and extinction on the descendants of one parent for a long enough time and the result is *not* a uniform spread of forms and *not* a simple linear series. It is little clusters of very similar forms (species of a genus) gathered into larger, more separated clusters (genera of a family), and those into larger still — **groups subordinate to groups**, with the levels marked out by extinct intermediates.

That is exactly the arrangement naturalists had been describing for a century under the name of the Natural System, and had treated as a mysterious plan. On Darwin's view it is nothing mysterious: classification is **genealogy**. Beings resemble each other in the degree to which they share descent, and the ranks of classification record how long ago the branching happened and how thoroughly the connecting forms have been swept away.

Darwin closes the chapter with the great tree image. The green, budding twigs are living species; the branches below them, the extinct species from which the living descended. Limb divides into limb and twig into twig; buds are far more numerous than the boughs they will ever become; of the many twigs that flourished when the tree was a mere bush, only two or three survive as great branches bearing all the rest. So too with the species that lived in ages past: very few have left living, modified descendants. The dead and broken branches, buried in the crust of the earth, are the extinct orders and families we know only as fossils. "As buds give rise by growth to fresh buds, and these, if vigorous, branch out and overtop on all sides many a feebler branch, so by generation I believe it has been with the great Tree of Life."

---

## Summary of the chain

1. Competition is fiercest between the most similar forms.
2. Therefore the most divergent descendants of a species do best, and diversified descendants can occupy more places and increase in numbers — the **principle of divergence**.
3. The crowding of many dissimilar species onto a small plot, and the yield of mixed sowings, show that diversity itself increases the amount of life supported.
4. Naturalised species belonging disproportionately to genera new to the country show the same thing on a continental scale.
5. Divergence preserves the extremes; **extinction** removes the intermediates and the parent forms.
6. The joint result over long ages is groups subordinate to groups — the Natural System — and the branching Tree of Life.
